Can You See the First Shooting Stars of 2027?

Episode 53 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌠
The Quadrantid meteor shower peaks the night of January 3 to 4, 2027, under a thin crescent Moon. Up to about 120 meteors an hour from very dark skies, but the peak lasts only a few hours. How and when to watch, and the mystery of where they come from.

segments.text: Want to see up to a hundred shooting stars an hour? Look up tomorrow night.
Tomorrow night, January third to fourth, the Quadrantid meteor shower reaches its peak.
segments.headline: Peak: night of Jan 3–4

segments.text: Under very dark skies, it can produce up to around one hundred twenty meteors an hour.
But there's a catch. The peak is short. Only about six hours. Timing matters.
Good news this year: the Moon is just a thin crescent, so its light won't wash out the meteors.
segments.headline: A thin Moon this year

segments.text: Best time: after midnight and before dawn. Look toward the north-east sky, and the higher in the north you live, the better.
segments.headline: After midnight, look northeast

segments.text: Get away from city lights, dress warm, lie back, and give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust. No telescope needed.
segments.headline: No telescope needed

segments.text: Most meteor showers come from comets. The Quadrantids come from an object called twenty-oh-three E H one, which may be a dead comet that stopped glowing.
segments.headline: From a dead comet?

segments.text: And the name? It comes from a constellation that no longer exists, Quadrans Muralis, a wall-mounted quadrant once used by astronomers.
segments.headline: A lost constellation
